tagline: Ghana's capital coast, its port twin a congested road away
summary: Accra, Ghana's capital, stretches along the Gulf of Guinea beside its industrial port twin of Tema, about thirty kilometres east. The two cities are joined by the country's busiest and most congested road corridor, while the coast between and beyond them — the historic James Town fishing harbour, the Volta estuary at Ada, and the Keta lagoon further east — frames a waterfront of fishing communities and emerging leisure. The Gulf of Guinea surf makes the open coast more exposed than a sheltered bay, but the Accra–Tema axis, the lagoon systems, and the capital's dense, app-comfortable population give the corridor a role in a connected marine network. Today no organised passenger-vessel layer works the coast — the Accra–Tema corridor and the lagoons are entirely road-bound.

transit_planning: Ghana's transport investment has centred on the Accra–Tema motorway and BRT pilots; the coast and lagoons remain served only by fishing craft and informal boats. A structured marine layer adds the capital–port coastal corridor and the lagoon links that road schemes do not reach.

competitive_landscape: The Accra–Tema coast has no organised passenger-vessel operator; the corridor is entirely road-bound and the lagoons are served by informal fishing craft. Ride-hail apps are mature on land but no player bridges the water. The open-coast surf raises the operational bar, but the corridor and lagoon demand are real and wholly unserved.
seasonality: The Gulf of Guinea surf is a year-round factor, strongest during the rainy seasons (April–June and September–October); the sheltered lagoons stay workable through the year while open-coast legs are swell-gated. The drier Harmattan months (December–February) offer the calmest open-water windows.
regulatory_note: Ghana's maritime passenger operations fall under the Ghana Maritime Authority; coastal and lagoon passenger craft sit within domestic licensing, coordinated with the Tema and Accra port authorities for harbour approaches. The Gulf-of-Guinea security context favours transparent, scheduled, well-documented operations close to shore.

precedents.why_it_matters: An established waterfront heritage anchor a coastal circuit can serve.
Sheltered lagoon systems with leisure demand served only by informal boats — a natural fit for a scheduled water layer.
